analysis.one_liner: Bans manufacture and sale of semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines over ten rounds, grandfathering existing guns.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 30, 2025 with 42 Senate cosponsors and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess certain semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns, and any ammunition magazine holding more than ten rounds. People who already own these guns could keep them, though they would have to store them securely, and a licensed dealer would have to run a background check before a private sale of a grandfathered rifle. Hunting rifles, manually operated guns, .22-caliber rimfires, and a long list of named exempt firearms would stay legal, as would guns sold to police and other government users.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities exposed to mass shootings, since the bill outlaws the manufacture and sale of the types of semiautomatic rifles most often used in them. Anyone who wants the federal government to treat gun regulation as constitutional 'for other purposes' — the bill's stated purpose includes declaring the right to keep and bear arms 'not unlimited' — also gains a legal framework for that argument.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a crime to knowingly import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon or a magazine holding more than ten rounds [S2][S3].

Lets current owners keep their weapons, but requires them to be stored securely so that people legally barred from having guns cannot reach them, and requires a dealer background check before a private sale of a grandfathered semiautomatic assault weapon [S2][S3].

Exempts manually operated bolt, pump, lever, and slide-action guns, permanently inoperable guns, antiques, rimfire-only guns, a long list of named hunting and sporting firearms, and guns used by law enforcement and nuclear-material security [S2][S3].
Allows states and local governments to use existing Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds to pay people who turn in covered weapons and magazines through buyback programs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and dealers lose the ability to make and sell the semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns on the banned list and any new magazine over ten rounds — a large share of the modern sporting and self-defense market. Existing owners of covered guns face a new secure-storage duty with criminal penalties, and private transfers of grandfathered rifles require a dealer background check; magazines over ten rounds already owned can be kept but not sold or given away.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and some owners

drawbacks.text: The definition of a banned weapon is based on feature combinations — a detachable magazine plus a pistol grip, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud — and on any magazine over ten rounds, so it sweeps in common firearms beyond the military-style rifles most people picture, including ordinary pistols whose standard magazines hold more than ten rounds [S3].

Because all covered weapons already in private hands are grandfathered, millions of them would remain in circulation for decades, and grandfathered rifles could still be resold with a background check, so the bill restricts future supply more than it reduces the guns that already exist [S2][S3].

Owners who fail to store a grandfathered weapon securely face criminal liability if someone prohibited from owning guns could access it, a duty that falls on households regardless of whether any harm occurs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the supply of the weapon types most associated with mass shootings while leaving hunting and manually operated firearms untouched, which is a deliberate narrowing meant to keep the ban within accepted gun ownership. Its honest weaknesses are definitional breadth — feature-based tests and the ten-round magazine line catch many ordinary handguns — and the grandfather clause, which means its effect on gun violence would build slowly over years rather than immediately. Supporters would trade those costs for cutting off future sales; opponents see the breadth itself as the problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on day one, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, no movement toward the floor.

narrative.text: Senator Adam Schiff introduced the bill on April 30, 2025, with 42 cosponsors — 41 of the 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 2 independents — and it was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1][S4][S5].
The action history shows no activity after the referral: no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled [S5].
No Republican senator has cosponsored the bill, and Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats and control the committee agenda [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, gun manufacturers and dealers, who keep the existing market for these firearms, and the Senate majority, which has faced no floor vote on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and sellers, so far

sides.party_line_note: All 43 Senate supporters are Democrats or independents — 41 of 45 Democrats and 1 of 2 independents signed on — and not a single Republican cosponsor; Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats and control the committee and floor agendas.

industries.note: The bill outlaws manufacturing and importing the semiautomatic rifles, pistols, shotguns, and parts on its list plus any new magazine over ten rounds — a large share of the modern sporting and self-defense market. Manufacturers keep their hunting, bolt-action, lever-action, rimfire, and named-exempt product lines, but lose their fastest-selling segment [S3].

Dealers could no longer sell new covered weapons or magazines, cutting inventory and sales. They would gain a mandated service, however: private transfers of grandfathered rifles would have to run through a dealer background check [S2][S3].

Owners keep what they have — no confiscation — but take on a secure-storage duty with criminal penalties, background-checked private sales, and magazines that can be kept but never resold. The value of grandfathered weapons could also shift as supply ends [S2][S3].

analysis.trajectory: Very likely to die without a vote. Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats, chair the Judiciary Committee, and no Republican has signed on, so the bill is unlikely to get a hearing, a markup, or floor time in this Congress — the same path most recent assault weapons bans have followed.
